articles.title: A former military airfield in Berlin was saved from redevelopment; now people picnic, cycle and garden on its giant runways
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Cities throughout the world constantly grapple with what to do with land left behind by dying industries, closed military facilities and obsolete infr.
articles.body: Cities throughout the world constantly grapple with what to do with land left behind by dying industries, closed military facilities and obsolete infrastructure. They often turn to housing or commercial development just because no better idea arrives in time. Berlin was facing precisely that conundrum after one of its most historically significant sites, a large Cold War-era airport in the centre of the city, stopped running flights altogether, igniting a protracted and often contentious debate about what should replace it.Tempelhof Airport opened in the late 1920s and quickly became one of Europe’s busiest airports. It took on international importance during the Berlin Blockade of 1948 and 1949, when Allied aircraft used its runways to supply the isolated western part of the city, landing as frequently as every 90 seconds at the height of the airlift. The airport continued to operate for decades after that, through hijackings and changing political borders and the building of newer airports elsewhere in the city, until commercial flights were finally stopped in October 2008 to consolidate air traffic at Berlin's new international airport.An area in the middle of the cityIn 2010, instead of shutting down the unused airfield, city officials opened the property to the public, allowing local residents to freely explore its wide-open runways and grassy verges for the first time in the area’s history. According to Tempelhofer Feld, the park’s official visitor information, it is now around 300 hectares in size, an area comparable in size to Central Park in New York, among the larger open spaces found in any major European city centre. That much open land soon caught the attention of city authorities looking for space to ease Berlin's tight housing market.Officials said much of the field could be left open and development could begin, and proposals for new residential neighbourhoods, commercial structures and a massive public library along the boundaries of the land circulated. In 2011, a grass-roots organisation, 100% Tempelhofer Feld, was formed to resist any construction, stating that the value of the land as open public space exceeded the benefits of construction on the edges. The group spent several years collecting support for a city-wide referendum on the question.Balloting settled the questionThat campaign resulted in a referendum held in May 2014, where locals were asked to vote on whether any part of the field may be developed. Official results from the Berlin state parliament indicated that 739,124 Berliners, about 64 percent of those who voted, backed keeping the whole pitch just as it was, clearing the 25 percent turnout quorum required under German referendum law and easily beating the development options put forward by city officials. The decision was legally binding under German referendum law, meaning the outcome prompted the city to abandon its development plans and instead establish specific legislation conserving the site permanently.In the weeks following the vote, a law was passed, officially called the Law for the Preservation of Tempelhof Field, which is still in effect today and specifically prohibits large-scale development projects on the field but allows carefully supervised community projects to continue to operate within its bounds. It is a rare example of a popular vote directly binding an official municipal development plan in a major European capital.Runways to picnicsThe former airfield is now one of the most popular public spaces in Berlin. Cyclists use the long runways, kite fliers enjoy the open skies, and families have picnics on the grass that previously lined active taxiways. On the eastern edge of the site is the Allmende Kontor, an intercultural community garden where hundreds of residents grow vegetables, herbs and flowers in more than 250 raised beds. It remains one of the site's most visible community projects.What started as a planning dispute became a case study in how residents can shape decisions about their own public land. The debate over the field’s future has sometimes re-emerged since 2014, but for now the runways where planes once hauled supplies into a besieged city are precisely what voters intended them to be: open, vacant and fully public.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Drug deaths rise sharply in Scotland as figures remain worst in Europe
articles.summary: The figure rose by 11% last  year, bringing the total deaths in a decade to more than 11,000.
articles.body:
Deaths related to illicit drugs rose by 11% in Scotland last year to 1,133 as the country struggles to tackle the worst fatality rate in Europe.

National Records of Scotland (NRS) said the figure for 2025 was 116 higher than the previous year, bringing the total deaths in a decade to more than 11,000.

After adjusting for age, there were 214 drug-related deaths per million people.

NRS defines drug-related deaths as those where the underlying cause was drug poisoning, a controlled substance was in the body at the time of death, and drug use led directly to the death.

Efforts to save lives over the past year have been hampered by criminal gangs mixing powerful synthetic opioids such as nitazenes with existing drugs including heroin, cocaine and fake Valium pills.

Nitazenes were implicated in 247 deaths in 2025 - more than 22% of the total. The figure had more than trebled from 76 deaths the previous year.

Opiates and opioids, such as heroin, continued to be the most common type of drug implicated in deaths, accounting for 78% of the total.

Cocaine was implicated in 52% of deaths, the highest figure since NRS began publishing specific data in 2008.

NRS said the increase in deaths - which came after a 13% fall in 2024 - had been driven by a rise in deaths of male drug users. This increased by 19%, while the rate of female deaths fell by 5%.

The rate of drug-related deaths in the most deprived areas of Scotland was 15 times as high as in the least deprived areas.

The average age of death has increased from 32 in 2000 to 46 years in 2025.

Over a five-year period from 2021-25, Glasgow recorded the highest average death rate at 380 per million, followed by 340 per million in Dundee and 310 per million in North Ayrshire.

When comparing Scotland with the rest of Europe, NRS measures the death rate among 15-64 year olds - which was 277 per million in 2025.

The next highest rate in Europe was Estonia with 112 deaths per million in 2024, the most recent year for which figures are available from the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA).

Scotland's death rate in 2024 was 246 per million.

NRS says its methodology produces "similar" outcomes to EUDA's count of "drug-induced deaths", with the caveat that the two methods use slightly different lists of drugs.

When comparing Scotland with the rest of the UK, NRS uses a wider measure of age-adjusted drug poisoning deaths.

This includes all deaths where the underlying cause was listed as mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance abuse or poisoning by drugs whether accidental, intentional, of unknown intent or as a result of assault.

The most recent comparable data from 2024 shows that Scotland had an age-adjusted death rate of 216 per million compared with 91 for England, 140 for Wales and 135 for Northern Ireland.

Catriona Matheson, professor of substance use at Stirling University, said the "deeply concerning" increase in deaths was being driven by significant changes in the drug market - including the growth of nitazenes.

She told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that their potency was unpredictable and that some could be 50 times stronger than heroin.

"People are not expecting that in the drugs that they're taking," she said.

"They may be buying what they think is heroin and in fact it may contain several other substances in it."

Matheson said an increase in "polydrug use" in recent years, where people take more than one substance, had contributed to the problem and could prove to be lethal.

Kirsten Horsburgh, chief executive of the Scottish Drugs Forum, said the link between deprivation, health inequalities and drug-related deaths was "really stark".

"The risk is we become fixed on chasing individual substances in an unregulated market and we lose sight of the individual circumstances that are related to that," she said.

"Drugs don't explain the extraordinary inequality and social disparity that we see in these deaths.

"Drug-related deaths are an extremely visible manifestation of who gets to live long and healthy lives."

Alcohol and Drugs Minister Maree Todd said the rise in deaths was "deeply concerning and unacceptable".

"The increase in deaths involving cocaine, and the continued threat from dangerous synthetic opioids like nitazenes, must drive more coordinated action across the country," she said.

Todd said the government had taken "important steps" - including funding more than 1,100 residential rehabilitation placements last year - but that it was clear much more needed to be done.

She said the government's new strategic plan would deepen links between treatment, housing and other services, and target support at the communities most at risk. The country's first local drug-checking service will open in Glasgow next month.

Scottish Labour's health spokesperson Jackie Baillie said the figures were "a damning indictment of the Scottish government's failure to support some of the most marginalised people in Scotland".

"They must take responsibility for this crisis and deliver joined-up action to save lives and help people recover," she said.

Victor Currie, Reform UK Scotland's spokesman, said the government had "given up on getting addicts into recovery and settled instead for managing the death toll".

"The SNP has evidently run out of ideas, run out of interest and frankly run out of excuses," he said.

Scottish Conservative spokesman Miles Briggs said the SNP's approach to tackling Scotland's drugs deaths crisis had "catastrophically failed".

"They must shut down their flagship Thistle facility in Glasgow and ditch any plans for more state-sponsored drug taking at drug consumption rooms," he said.

Scottish Green spokesperson Kayleigh Kinross-O'Neill said a major expansion of harm reduction and treatment services was needed, including safe consumption facilities, drug checking, heroin-assisted treatment and stabilisation services.

Scottish Liberal Democrat leader Alex Cole-Hamilton called for a national rollout of safer drugs consumption centres and funding for "long-overdue" drug checking services.

articles.title: 'Differing views normal part of deliberation': EC responds after report flags rift over SIR
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Wednesday responded to a report flagging differences within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Wednesday responded to a report flagging differences within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), saying that “differing views and observations” among its members were a normal part of deliberation, while stressing that all final decisions were taken "unanimously"."The ECI is a constitutional body that functions under the strict mandate of Article 324 of the Constitution, statutory rules and established institutional conventions. The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour. All actions of ECI have been in accordance of laws and instructions of the Commission," EC said in an official statement."All official orders, decisions and administrative directions issued by the Commission carry full legal sanctions and follow established statutory procedures under The Chief Election Commissioner and Other election commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023," it added.The poll panel said that differing views are normal part of decision making process before a final decision is taken"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorized to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," it said.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over the period of 10 months give only one part of the picture"Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said."The Election Commission of India remains fully committed to executing its constitutional duties with complete integrity, recognizing its vital role in advancing our democracy," it added.The clarification came after an Indian Express report triggered a row by claiming that the two Election Commissioners had raised objections to the Commission's decisions 14 times over the past 10 months during the SIR exercise.Meanwhile, opposition sharpened its attack on the Election Commission over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi also revived his "vote chori" charge against the Election Commission and accused election officials of committing "treason."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2025, a hiker found a frightened dog in Oregon woods; he turned a tripod into a leash, filmed the rescue for TikTok and reunited him with his owner
articles.summary: US News: Jason Hawkins was on a routine hike to an Oregon hot spring when two women at the trailhead asked whether he had seen a missing dog. Hawkins was not s.
articles.body: Jason Hawkins was on a routine hike to an Oregon hot spring when two women at the trailhead asked whether he had seen a missing dog. Hawkins was not searching for a pet himself, but the question stayed with him as he began walking into the woods. About a quarter of a mile into the hike, he spotted a small dog hiding among the trees. The frightened animal ran away whenever Hawkins tried to approach, but eventually became too exhausted to keep fleeing.According to Hawkins, the dog had escaped from its owners' vehicle and disappeared into the woods. By the time the hiker found him, the animal was tired, frightened and reluctant to be picked up. Hawkins did not have his usual hiking equipment with him, but he happened to be carrying a camera tripod. That small piece of equipment became the key to getting the dog safely back to the trailhead.When a tripod became a leashHawkins first tried to calm the dog by approaching slowly and speaking to him. He offered water, although the animal was not interested. Once he was close enough, he noticed the dog was wearing a collar. Instead of attempting to carry him, Hawkins attached the clip from his camera tripod to the collar and created what amounted to an improvised lead.The improvised solution worked almost immediately. As reported by Hawkins to PEOPLE, once the dog realised the slight pulling action on the rope, he seemed to realise that he was being led somewhere. The dog stopped resisting and walked beside him toward the trailhead. Hawkins eventually wrapped the dog in his jacket after using his towel near a river.The episode shows that a frightened lost dog may not behave like a familiar pet. A dog separated from its owner can become disoriented and may run from people attempting to help. Research published in the Journal of Veterinary Behaviour has compared shelter and pet dogs when approached by an unfamiliar experimenter, and found shelter dogs showed more fear-appeasement behaviour, including tail down, ears down and crouching, while still often staying close to the person. The authors say that pattern may reflect the stressful conditions and limited human contact typical of shelters.A message finally reached the ownersBut the difficulty of getting the dog out of the woods wasn’t all there was to it; Hawkins had to locate the family. Since the dog had a tag on it, he tried contacting the phone number that was written on the tag. But due to bad cell reception in the area, he could only send a text message via the satellite network.A short while after this, the owners finally got to the trailhead. They had been searching for quite some time after their pet had run away from the car and disappeared in the woods. The moment the dog’s owner saw him was very emotional. According to Hawkins, the lady was crying and did not know how to express herself when she took her pet, who was comfortable enough to be held by her.Research into lost-pet recovery also helps explain why identification can be so important. A study in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association found that dogs wearing licence tags had a higher likelihood of being recovered, while contacting animal agencies and posting signs were among the other approaches used successfully by owners. The presence of identification on Hawkins' rescued dog gave him a direct route to its family once communication became possible.From quiet rescue to viral storyThe rescue was partly captured on camera, and Hawkins uploaded the video to TikTok. According to PEOPLE, the video was said to have reached 1.2 million views and 10,000 comments. The online attention mattered less to Hawkins than what happened at the trailhead. The most gratifying aspect for him was seeing how relieved the owner looked after all the uncertainty. Even though he left home without his usual gear for hiking, a tripod, a collar, and some patience were enough to assist in the rescue of the scared dog.The rescue showed how a casual encounter can quickly turn into something more when someone pays attention. The women who warned Hawkins about the lost dog at the trailhead probably would not have known where to look. Hawkins noticed a dog that might otherwise have gone unnoticed in the brush, and the collar helped identify it. This search, which started with a query on a hiking trail in Oregon, ended with a distraught owner holding her dog again. What stands out about the rescue is the unlikely clue from a camera tripod, but patience, observation and a simple ID tag made it possible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday delivered a split verdict on whether the challenge to the law governing the appointment of the Chief Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday delivered a split verdict on whether the challenge to the law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners should be considered by a Constitution Bench.Under the law, the selection panel comprises the Prime Minister, a Union cabinet minister and the leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha.Justice Dipankar Datta countered the Centre's argument against the collegium system for appointing judges, saying the perception that "judges appoint judges" is a myth.Justice Datta also said that there was no need to refer the case to the constitution bench and a two-judge bench can examine its validity.Read also: SC split over CEC appointment law, differences over Constitution Bench referralLast month, underscoring the need for an independent and impartial process for selection of the chief election commissioner and election commissioners, Supreme Court said Election Commission must not only act independently but must also be seen to act independently. The court questioned why Parliament, while framing the law, decided not to include Chief Justice of India in the selection panel.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma said the CJI was part of selection panels for CBI director and Lokpal, and asked what could be the reason for excluding him from the process of selecting CEC and ECs — posts that are among the most important for a democracy. The court reserved its verdict on the Centre’s plea that the matter be referred to a constitution bench.The court is hearing challenges to the constitutional validity of the 2023 Act, under which CEC and ECs are appointed by President on the recommendation of a selection committee consisting of PM, leader of the opposition, and a Union Cabinet minister nominated by PM. articles.title: In 2013, a Los Angeles man’s VW Beetle vanished; one stranger sent a photo, and another used Google Street View to find it five days later
articles.summary: US News: In April 2013, Jason Torchinsky walked outside his Los Angeles home and discovered that his yellow 1973 Volkswagen Beetle was missing. He had owned th.
articles.body: In April 2013, Jason Torchinsky walked outside his Los Angeles home and discovered that his yellow 1973 Volkswagen Beetle was missing. He had owned the car since he was 18 and had kept it for more than a decade, making its disappearance particularly distressing. At first, he wondered whether it had been towed, but he soon realised that the vehicle had been stolen. What followed was an unusual internet-assisted search that used a single photograph, a handful of visual clues and Google Street View to locate the missing car within five days.According to KSL News, the search ended five days after Torchinsky discovered his Beetle was missing, when reader Mike sent him the location he had identified using Google Maps. Torchinsky travelled to the spot in El Sereno and found his 1973 Volkswagen Beetle, but the car had been heavily stripped. Its headlights, luggage rack, radio and engine were missing, with the total damage estimated at $3,000.A photograph becomes a location puzzleThe photo did not show a street address. Instead, it depicted the Beetle parked beside a mint-green house, which was surrounded by a white wrought-iron fence. There was a blue Toyota FJ Cruiser in the vicinity and a unique hillside in the background. These details gave Mike the clues he needed to narrow down the location using Google Maps and Street View.He compared Los Angeles streets with the photograph, looking for the surrounding features rather than searching for the Beetle itself. He focused on the shape of the hillside, the house and the parked vehicle. After about 30 minutes of searching, he found a location that appeared to match the photograph.The blue FJ Cruiser provided an additional confirmation that he had found the right place. Google describes Street View as a collection of panoramic imagery captured from vehicles travelling through public areas. The images are associated with geographic locations, allowing users to explore streets virtually rather than simply viewing them on a conventional map.The stolen Beetle was still thereAccording to Jason Torchinsky’s account in Jalopnik, the search ended five days after he discovered his Beetle was missing, when the reader who had identified the location sent him the address. Torchinsky travelled to the spot and found his 1973 Volkswagen Beetle, but the car had been heavily stripped. Its headlights, roof rack, radio and engine were missing, while other parts of the vehicle had also been damaged. Despite its condition, the discovery meant that the car he had owned since he was 18 had finally been located.The recovery was possible because several independent sources of information came together. The online appeal from Torchinsky spread the description of the car, while the photograph provided evidence about the location to which the Beetle had been taken, and Mike was able to use this information to locate it. This task was closer to solving a geography puzzle than searching for a car.An early example of crowdsourced sleuthingTorchinsky’s Beetle case also showed how online communities can help solve a puzzle that initially seemed to offer little to go on. It was not necessary to use any high-tech police computer database or a vehicle tracking system. What helped was the information each person contributed: one shared photographs and details about the car, another had taken pictures of it, and Mike realised the backdrop could be matched with Street View images.However, there was one critical limitation about the technology too. It is important to note that Google’s Street View is not live surveillance; Google says the imagery is captured at specific times and may differ from what is physically there when someone later visits. In Torchinsky's situation, the imagery was just sufficient to help the person find the street.The stolen 40-year-old Volkswagen came with only a few clues: its colour, a house, the slope of a hill, and another car parked nearby. But a stranger who investigated all these clues was able to pinpoint the exact location where the owner recovered his car within an hour spent browsing around the streets of Los Angeles via Street View. This has often been cited as an example of how ordinary online tools can have unexpected uses.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Forced to consume pesticide': Telangana lecturer kills engineering student after she befriended another man
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: An engineering student who had gone to a coal mine for a 12-day internship was allegedly killed by her former lecturer after he learnt that.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: An engineering student who had gone to a coal mine for a 12-day internship was allegedly killed by her former lecturer after he learnt that she had been sexually exploited by an overman at the mine, police said.The victim (20), native of a village in Sultanabad mandal, was allegedly forced to consume pesticide by her former lecturer, Jetty Naveen Kumar, on September 12. Police said Naveen Kumar later made her write a suicide note and tried to pass off the incident as suicide. She died while undergoing treatment at a government hospital on September 13.Peddapalli DCP Ram Reddy said police arrested Naveen Kumar in Godavarikhani on Sunday based on CCTV footage, call records and other technical evidence. Overman Bommakanthi Ravikumar (35), who was also arrested in connection with the sexual assault case, was remanded in judicial custody.According to police, the victim completed her diploma at Singareni Polytechnic in Naspur, Mancherial district, in 2022. Naveen Kumar, who was working as a contract lecturer at the college at the time, was also from Garrepalli. Their acquaintance grew into a close relationship, police said.Naveen Kumar, who was living separately from his wife following differences, allegedly assured the victim that he would marry her. She later joined Osmania University to pursue BE in Mining. After her family shifted to Godavarikhani, she joined a coal mine there in January for a 12-day internship as part of her course.Police said Ravikumar, who was working as an overman at the mine, introduced himself to the victim as a former student of Naspur Polytechnic and a student of Naveen Kumar. He allegedly began sexually harassing her.The victim subsequently complained to the Singareni management against Ravikumar. The management constituted a committee to inquire into the complaint and, according to police, concluded that Ravikumar was not at fault. Police said Ravikumar later sexually assaulted the victim.Naveen Kumar subsequently came to know about the relationship between the victim and Ravikumar and allegedly decided to kill her, police said.On September 12, Naveen Kumar allegedly picked up victim in his car and drove around with her before forcing her to consume pesticide. articles.body: Libra season is associated with relationships, balance, partnerships and the choices we make while dealing with other people. As per tropical astrology, this begins from September mid.But this year, the message is slightly different.It is not about keeping everyone happy. It is about understanding where you should adjust and where you should stop adjusting.For some signs, this will play out in relationships. For others, it can show up through career, money, family or personal priorities. October can also bring old conversations and unfinished matters back into focus, so don't be surprised if something you thought was settled suddenly needs another look.Here is what Libra season can mean for you.AriesRelationships need more attention. You may find yourself questioning whether the effort in a personal or professional partnership is genuinely equal. Couples can have important conversations, while singles may become clearer about what they will and will not accept anymore. Don't turn every disagreement into a battle. Sometimes the relationship matters more than proving who was right.TaurusYour daily routine needs a reset. Work can become demanding, and you may realise that your current schedule leaves very little time for yourself. Pay attention to sleep, food, exercise and the way you divide your responsibilities. Being capable of handling everything doesn't mean you should be handling everything.GeminiLove becomes interesting. Someone from the past may return, an old conversation could restart or you may simply begin looking at an existing connection differently. Creativity also improves, making this a good period for hobbies and personal projects. If someone returns, don't immediately assume they deserve another chance. First understand why they returned and whether anything has actually changed.CancerHome and family take centre stage. You may think about changing something in your house, relocating, dealing with property or resolving an ongoing family issue. The important thing is not to keep suppressing your feelings merely to maintain peace. A peaceful home is not one where nobody speaks about problems. It is one where problems can be discussed without damaging relationships.LeoCommunication becomes your biggest strength as well as your biggest responsibility. Meetings, messages, networking and important conversations can increase. Choose your words carefully, particularly when irritated. Also double-check important messages and documents before sending them. Not every thought needs an immediate voice.VirgoMoney becomes important. You may start thinking seriously about what you earn, what you charge and where your money actually goes. This is a useful time to review unnecessary expenses and reconsider purchases made mainly for appearances. Looking successful and becoming financially successful are two completely different things.LibraThis is your season, but that doesn't necessarily mean everything suddenly becomes easy. You may start questioning your appearance, relationships, priorities and even the version of yourself you've been presenting to others. Don't rush into a complete reinvention. You don't need to become a different person. You may simply need to stop being the version of yourself everyone else expects.ScorpioYou may want more privacy than usual. An old emotional issue, unfinished relationship or personal disappointment can return to your thoughts. Instead of immediately trying to fix everything, give yourself time to understand what you actually feel. Some chapters don't need another conversation. They simply need you to stop rereading them.SagittariusYour social circle becomes important. New people can enter your life, while some older friendships or professional connections may need reassessment. Pay attention to who genuinely supports your growth and who only appears when they need something. A bigger network isn't always a better network.CapricornCareer comes into focus. You may receive more responsibility, visibility or an opportunity to prove yourself. At the same time, disagreements with seniors or authority figures need careful handling. Don't allow ego to turn a manageable situation into a professional problem. You can stand your ground without turning every difference of opinion into a confrontation.AquariusYou may feel ready for something different. Travel, education, a new course, teaching, writing or exploring a completely different way of working can become attractive. This is a good time to expand your perspective, but don't rush into commitments without checking the practical details. Explore first. Commit after you understand what you're signing up for.PiscesMoney and trust become connected. Shared finances, loans, investments or financial responsibilities involving a partner may need discussion. Emotionally too, you may want greater honesty from someone close to you. Avoid keeping difficult subjects silent simply because you don't want an uncomfortable conversation.The larger message of Libra seasonLibra season often gets reduced to love, romance and relationships.But balance is much bigger than that.It is the balance between work and life, spending and saving, speaking and listening, giving and receiving, adjusting and standing your ground.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. articles.body: Self-taught teenager Daisha Auda from Logan, Queensland, has made television history by becoming the first Torres Strait Islander singer to reach the grand final of The Voice Australia. The 15-year-old singer earned a spot in the top four after a series of standout performances that won over both the judges and viewers across the country. Her run on the show marks a historic moment for First Nations representation on Australian commercial television.Standing out from the blind auditionAuda first caught the nation's attention during her blind audition, where she sang Lizzo's hit song "Cuz I Love You." Her vocal control and stage presence led all four celebrity judges to turn their chairs, each offering her a spot on their team. Reporting by local news outlet My City Logan revealed that Auda had never taken formal singing lessons before appearing on The Voice. Instead, she taught herself to sing at home, practicing daily, listening to recordings online, and getting guidance from her family. After the four-chair turn, Auda chose her first coach to help guide her through the early rounds, earning praise for her maturity and natural pitch despite having no formal training.Surviving elimination and finding a second chanceThe young singer's road to the grand final wasn't easy. During the knockout rounds, Auda faced elimination after her original coach chose another artist to move forward in the competition. However, her run on the show continued when another judge used a "steal" to save her from elimination, bringing her onto a new team. This move allowed Auda to move on to the live semi-finals, keeping her chances at the title alive. In the semi-final, Auda gave a powerful performance that earned her one of the four spots in the grand final.Representation and cultural impactAuda's advancement to the final marks the first time a Torres Strait Islander artist has reached the grand final in the history of The Voice Australia. According to coverage by Indigenous culture publication Style Up NIT, her achievement has sparked widespread pride in her home community of Logan and among First Nations communities across Australia. The milestone reflects the growing presence of young Indigenous talent in mainstream media. Speaking to local media about her time on the show, Auda said she hopes her journey will inspire other young people from regional areas and cultural backgrounds to pursue their goals in the arts, no matter their formal training or early setbacks.Preparing for the grand finaleThe upcoming grand final episode will see Auda perform alongside the three remaining finalists as they compete for the national title and a major recording contract. articles.title: In the 1990s, a blind Florida conservationist kept fighting for the Everglades; her organization helped win a $90 million fund to buy and protect endangered land in Miami-Dade County
articles.summary: US News: Marjory Stoneman Douglas was blind and facing health problems in the 1990s, but she was still involved with the environmental campaign that she had he.
articles.body: Marjory Stoneman Douglas was blind and facing health problems in the 1990s, but she was still involved with the environmental campaign that she had helped build decades earlier. Her organization was called Friends of the Everglades, and it worked with other conservation groups to support a Dade County environmental preservation plan that established a $90 million fund to buy and protect endangered land. The University of Miami’s digital exhibition on Douglas records the campaign as part of her ongoing work to preserve South Florida’s water and natural areas.The fight that began with the EvergladesDouglas had spent much of her public life arguing that the Everglades was a system that was essential to South Florida. Her 1947 book, The Everglades: River of Grass, helped bring wider attention to the region, and she later became one of the most persistent voices against projects that threatened its water flow. According to the University of Miami account, Douglas and other conservationists opposed plans for an Everglades jet port and argued that development in the area could damage the natural system. Their campaign succeeded and the proposed jet port was never built.Douglas went on to establish Friends of the Everglades and continued working on water-management issues, primarily focused on cleaning up and preserving the Kissimmee-Okeechobee-Everglades basin. Douglas argued that freshwater was directly tied to South Florida’s ability to support its population, rather than being an environmental concern separate from everyday life.She continued pressing that argument through public campaigns, legal challenges and appearances before officials, which kept the Everglades in discussions about South Florida’s growth and water policy. Her work also helped establish conservation as a long-term political issue in the region, rather than a temporary response to individual development projects.She was still involved at 100The University of Miami exhibition says that she supported several environmental initiatives during the 1980s, which included the Coastal Barrier Resources Act and Florida’s efforts to protect the Everglades. Douglas was blind and dealing with health problems by the 1990s, but Friends of the Everglades continued its work. The organization joined other environmental groups in campaigning for the Dade County Referendum Environmental Preservation plan, and the measure established a $90 million fund for acquiring and protecting environmentally endangered land in the county.The county says voters approved a property-tax increase between 1990 and 1992 so that they could fund the acquisition, protection and maintenance of environmentally endangered lands. The county’s current Environmentally Endangered Lands program says that it and its partners have since brought more than 20,700 acres into public ownership, while another 2,800 acres of natural land are managed within Miami-Dade County parks.Her work continued after the referendumDouglas died at her Coconut Grove home on May 14, 1998, aged 108, which is why she did not see the full development of the county’s land-protection program. The Florida Department of State notes that she had remained active in conservation for much of her life and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Bill Clinton in 1993.The $90 million fund came from a county referendum rather than from Douglas or Friends of the Everglades alone, but the University of Miami records the organization’s participation in the campaign while Douglas was still active despite her blindness and declining health. Miami-Dade’s program remains active today, with the county describing its purpose as protecting and conserving environmentally endangered lands across the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: A London air-raid shelter built for wartime protection now grows salad leaves underground, using LED lights instead of sunlight
articles.summary: US News: Thirty-three metres beneath Clapham High Street in south London, rows of green plants once grew inside tunnels that were originally built as a World W.
articles.body: Thirty-three metres beneath Clapham High Street in south London, rows of green plants once grew inside tunnels that were originally built as a World War II air-raid shelter. The Growing Underground project used hydroponics, artificial lighting and tightly controlled conditions to produce salad leaves and herbs without natural sunlight. The farm was developed in the former shelter by entrepreneurs Richard Ballard and Steven Dring and began operating commercially in the mid-2010s.From wartime shelter to underground farmThe tunnels were built during World War II as part of London’s network of deep-level air-raid shelters, and the Clapham site was large enough to accommodate thousands of people during bombing raids, but it later remained largely unused. Ballard encountered the tunnels while working on a film project and began considering whether the underground space could be used for food production. He and Dring eventually developed the Growing Underground concept and began testing the idea.Underground, the temperature and growing conditions could be managed without the daily changes in weather, sunlight and outdoor pests. By 2015, the former shelter had been converted into a working farm, and the University of Cambridge described it as the world’s first underground farm, with stacked racks of crops growing under banks of LED lights.No soil and no sunlightThe plants were grown hydroponically rather than in soil, and nutrients were delivered through water, while LED lights supplied the light required for photosynthesis. The farm produced crops including pea shoots, basil, coriander, parsley, salad rocket, radish and mustard plants. Cambridge researchers later worked with the farm to monitor conditions including temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, water use and light levels.Cambridge reported that some crops could be harvested roughly every 10 days, while the system used less water and space than conventional greenhouse production. The farm’s hydroponic setup used recycled materials, including wool carpet offcuts as growing mats.Cambridge researchers developed a digital twin of the farm to study the relationship between lighting, temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and plant growth. Their work found that optimisation reduced the time needed to grow some crops by as much as 50%, while average growing time fell by 7% and yields increased by 24%.The farm’s unusual location was part of the pointGrowing Underground was designed around the idea that food could be produced close to the people who would eat it. The Clapham tunnels were within London rather than on agricultural land outside the city, and the produce could be sent to nearby markets and restaurants after harvesting.A 2016 report by The Guardian described the tunnels as being about 120 feet underground and said the farm could produce up to 2,000 packs of herbs a day at that stage, which included pea shoots, rocket, red basil, radish, fennel and coriander. The project eventually became a case study in controlled-environment agriculture, particularly because it used infrastructure that had already existed rather than constructing a purpose-built underground facility.The University of Cambridge notes that the private company Growing Underground was dissolved in November 2023, and the farm therefore should not be described as an operating underground farm today. Its Clapham tunnels remain an example of how a wartime shelter was once repurposed for commercial food production under LED lighting.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Governments formed amid lapses unconstitutional’: Akhilesh Yadav attacks EC over reported internal dissent on SIR
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday questioned the functioning of the Election Commission, saying governments formed duri.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday questioned the functioning of the Election Commission, saying governments formed during a period when the poll panel was not acting impartially were “unconstitutional”.Addressing a press conference in Lucknow, Yadav referred to a report that said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and electoral roll procedures.Yadav said the Election Commission was regarded as an impartial institution and was expected to strengthen democracy. He questioned “on whose behalf” the poll panel was functioning if its own members were raising objections to its decisions.“This is dangerous for our democracy. This is an attempt to weaken our democracy,” he said.Yadav questions fairness of electionsThe SP chief said the Election Commission was a constitutional body and questioned who was “playing with” such an institution for the purpose of remaining in government.“What can you imagine now? Would the Election Commission have been fair? Would it have been impartial?” he asked.Yadav said the reported objections from within the poll panel raised questions about the functioning of an institution whose basic expectation was impartiality.“This means that the governments which have been formed during this period are unconstitutional governments,” he said, alleging that democracy had been “trampled upon”.In an earlier post on X, Yadav described the reported objections by the two Election Commissioners as “extremely serious news”.“It is extremely serious news that in the last 10 months, two Election Commissioners have recorded their objections 14 times to the wrong decisions of the Election Commission,” he said.“Making democracy a victim by becoming puppets of some people in power is a grave constitutional crime. It is no less than a conspiracy to destroy democracy,” Yadav said, urging the Supreme Court to take suo motu cognisance of the matter.Yadav alleges deletion of SP votersYadav also alleged that voters supporting the Samajwadi Party had been “systematically deleted” from electoral rolls and claimed no corrective action was taken after the issue was brought to the Election Commission's notice.“The Election Commission claims it will strengthen democracy. When such things are happening within the Election Commission itself, where can one place their trust? In the span of 10 months, various officials have written letters 14 times. Samajwadi Party voters were systematically deleted from the Election Commission's voters list. We brought this to the notice of the Election Commission, but no action was taken against anyone. Rampant malpractice was committed on a massive scale in the by-elections,” Yadav said.The Election Commission, however, said all its decisions, including those related to SIR, were taken unanimously with the approval of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the two other Election Commissioners.Responding to the report, the EC said written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks were standard practices within a multi-member constitutional body. It said all official orders and decisions carried full legal sanction and followed established statutory procedures.The commission said differing views were part of institutional deliberations before a final decision was taken. It also said it had introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken electoral reforms, including electoral-roll revision and SIR.Yadav targets UP governmentYadav also accused the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh of arbitrary governance.“The government is acting arbitrarily. It is dismantling every system. Those who believe in demolition and destruction—whether it comes to the law or the Constitution—simply do not care about anything. This government is trampling upon everyone’s dignity and self-respect,” he said.On Ayodhya, Yadav said the SP had never opposed construction of the Ram Temple but accused the BJP of displacing local residents through demolition drives.“We have never wanted to be an obstacle in the development of the Lord Shri Ram Temple in Ayodhya, nor will we ever be in the future. We will develop a far better city of Ayodhya than they ever could. They are snatching away the rights of the poor,” he said.The Election Commission controversy has also drawn criticism from other Opposition parties, with Congress MP Rahul Gandhi questioning the poll panel and CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged “vote chori”.Opposition parties had earlier moved motions seeking the removal of Gyanesh Kumar.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Michigan photographer Chanise Coyne, 46, has been sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a local family of more than $4.6 million through a child modelling scheme. Coyne pleaded guilty to wire fraud on May 19, 2026, after admitting that she falsely claimed the money would cover advance fees for the family's young daughter's participation in modelling events across the US. According to the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Coyne created fake text messages, emails and invoices to support the supposed modelling placements. She used the proceeds for personal expenses, including gambling and more than $200,000 in Taylor Swift concert tickets in Florida. The court ordered her to pay $4,669,962.76 in restitution and serve three years of supervised release.How Coyne carried out the $4.6 million modelling fraudAccording to federal prosecutors, Coyne falsely represented that the family’s payments would cover advance fees linked to their daughter’s participation in modelling events across the country. She created fraudulent records, including text messages, emails and invoices, to make the supposed opportunities appear legitimate. Coyne admitted that the money was not used to place the girl in a single modelling event. Instead, she diverted the funds for her personal benefit, according to the DOJ’s sentencing announcement.Gambling and expensive Taylor Swift concert ticketsFederal prosecutors said Coyne spent significant amounts of the fraud proceeds on gambling. She also used more than $200,000 to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets in Florida. The money obtained through the alleged modelling arrangements was redirected towards personal spending rather than the opportunities promised to the family. Coyne was arrested and charged in February 2026. The indictment included seven counts of wire fraud and five counts of money laundering. Prosecutors alleged that she created false records connected to the modelling placements and impersonated a third party. The indictment also described significant gambling expenditures, including transactions involving the online sports betting platform FanDuel. Coyne later pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud.Coyne pleaded guilty in May 2026On May 19, 2026, Coyne admitted that she obtained more than $4.6 million from a local family by falsely claiming that the funds would cover advance fees for their daughter’s participation in modelling events.She also admitted creating fake communications and invoices connected to the supposed placements. The DOJ confirmed that none of the money was used to place the girl in a modelling event.Photographer receives five-year prison sentenceA federal court sentenced Coyne on September 22, 2026, to five years in prison. She was also ordered to pay $4,669,962.76 in restitution and serve three years of supervised release after her imprisonment. US Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr. said Coyne used a child’s aspirations to conceal a multimillion-dollar fraud against the family. Jennifer Runyan, special agent in charge of the FBI Detroit Field Office, said the scheme exploited the family’s trust for financial gain.Earlier controversy involving Santa Claus photographyBefore the federal case became public, Coyne’s photography business was involved in a separate controversy concerning a cancelled Santa Claus photography session in November 2024.FOX 2 Detroit reported that Coyne cancelled the sessions and claimed that the Santa involved had mpox. The station also spoke to the Santa, who showed messages related to the dispute. According to the report, Coyne returned the money to the Macomb Township family involved.Customers reported complaints about cancelled sessionsFOX 2 Detroit reported mixed online reviews of Coyne’s photography business, including complaints from customers who said their sessions had been cancelled and that they had not received refunds. The station also reported the existence of a private Facebook group named Chanise Coyne Scam Victims, which had 99 members when the report was published in May 2026. These complaints formed part of the wider public controversy surrounding her photography business but were separate from the federal charges described in the indictment.The FBI investigated the multimillion-dollar fraud scheme. articles.title: Concerns Herefordshire will not benefit from £2 bus cap
articles.summary: Councillor Justine Peberdy says Yeomans Travel and Sargeants Brothers have not committed to the cap.
articles.body:
Herefordshire's two largest bus operators have not yet committed to the flat £2 fare being urged by the government, according to council bosses.

Ledbury councillor Justine Peberdy said the price cap scheme "will not benefit Herefordshire unless our operators choose to participate in it".

Yeomans Travel and Sargeants Brothers, who between them operate a majority of the county's services, did not participate in the current £3 bus fare and there were concerns they would not participate in the new scheme, she said. Yeomans has said it was waiting for more information before deciding.

The bus fare cap in England will revert to £2, from the current £3 from January.

Peberdy, who chairs a group which looks into how the county's bus services can be improved, confirmed Bromyard-based DRM did plan to participate.

Independent councillor Nick Mason said it would be "horrendous" if the rest of the country took part but fares in Herefordshire cost more.

Tammy Gerber of local campaign group Buses4Us said the difference between capped and uncapped fares could run to £1,200 a year for someone commuting five days a week in the county.

"Herefordshire's operators need to get with the programme before January 2027 and not leave young people to find out the hard way that they've been left behind," she said.

Sergeants currently has 24 routes listed on the Herefordshire Council website, chiefly in and around Hereford and westwards towards and into Wales.

Yeomans Travel meanwhile operates 31 routes including many serving villages around Hereford, to Leominster and the north and also the southwest of the county.

A Yeomans spokesperson said that with the details of the scheme "still evolving", the support on offer from the government would depend on data it had yet to submit.

"Consequently, a final decision on participation cannot be made at this point," they said, adding: "We do not expect to receive the government's proposal until late November."

Sargeants was also contacted for comment.

articles.title: Diddington solar farm to power Anglian Water facility approved
articles.summary: The plans are approved despite objections about the use of greenfield sites.
articles.body:
A solar farm expected to power a water treatment facility has been approved despite concerns about the use of greenfield sites.

The project, on land off Vicarage Lane in Diddington in Cambridgeshire, is expected to cover 45 hectares (111 acres) of farmland, making it equivalent to 63 football pitches.

Huntingdonshire District Council approved the plans but parish councils in Buckden and Southoe and Midloe objected, stating greenfield sites should not be used until other options, including brownfield sites, had been "fully utilised".

Cell Energy Limited, the company behind the plans, said it had an agreement with Anglian Water to provide the company with energy.

Edmund Thornhill, a local landowner who spoke in favour of the plans, told a meeting of the council's development and management committee on Monday: "There needs to be careful consideration around best use of land even if that use is for a finite period — the farm already provides food, housing and space for nature. We want to support energy production as well over the poorest land.

"The scheme would provide diversified income to help fund moving to more regenerative agriculture on the rest of the farm."

The project is expected to operate for 45 years and produce 35MW of electricity.

The Local Democracy Reporting Service said an underground cable would be built to Anglian Water's facility at Grafham Water, which the planning application said was a "very significant energy user".

Buckden Parish Council and Southoe and Midloe Parish Council both argued "there should be no more solar farms on greenfield sites until all residential and commercial roof spaces and brownfield sites have been fully utilised".

Jon Neigh, Conservative councillor, said he could not see a reason to object to the plans.

Green councillor Lara Davenport-Ray said renewable energy projects were "really important".

The plans were approved with 12 voting in favour and one against.

articles.summary: The Board of Peace, set up by US President Donald Trump, will reportedly unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza on Wednesday, outlining
articles.body: The Board of Peace, set up by US President Donald Trump, will reportedly unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza on Wednesday, outlining 66 projects focused on rebuilding infrastructure, restoring essential services, reviving the economy and establishing post-war governance.The plan, prepared over the past year by officials from the Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government, includes funding for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force.But its implementation will depend on cooperation from Israel and Hamas. Israel has agreed in principle to some elements of the proposal but has refused to begin implementing it, while Hamas has agreed in principle to disarm but the process has yet to be tested.The Board of Peace hopes the recovery process can begin after Israel's October 27 election and the formation of a new government. However, the election could result in political deadlock, potentially further delaying the proposal."The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said.The proposal estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade.Infrastructure accounts for the largest share of the six-month plan, at roughly $1 billion. It includes about $400 million for temporary shelters, $275 million for rubble and unexploded ordnance clearance, $50 million for hospital rehabilitation and $30 million for road repairs.The plan also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar-power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects.Security-related projects account for roughly $885 million, including $275 million for a permanent site in Rafah capable of supporting 5,000 personnel from the International Stabilization Force and $140 million to recruit, train, equip and deploy a multinational security contingent.Another $120 million would go towards mobilising Palestinian police, while $20 million would fund a weapons buy-back programme offering incentives for Hamas and other armed groups to surrender weapons and ammunition.The plan also allocates about $400 million for insulated caravans for Palestinians currently living in tents. Separately, the UAE would fund a pilot "Emirati Neighborhood" in Rafah designed to house 50,000 people, while about $300 million would go towards health, education and welfare programmes.The proposal also includes a digital ID system, digital payments, 4G connectivity, electronic health and education systems, grants to restart small businesses and a new Gaza investment fund.The Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government say the recovery should be Palestinian-led and based on "Palestinian ownership".The two sides have yet to secure the full $2.45 billion required for the six-month programme, although Board of Peace officials said the entire amount would not be needed immediately.Representatives from 35 countries are expected to attend Wednesday's briefing, including officials from the European Union and several of its member states. Trump's senior adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are also expected to speak.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: One Iowa school lands in U.S. News' top 100 universities for 2027
articles.summary: One Iowa school earned a top-100 ranking in U.S. News' 2027 Best Colleges list. Here's where Iowa colleges and universities placed.
articles.body:
One Iowa university ranked in the top 100 schools for U.S. News' Best Colleges list.

U.S. News & World Report has released its 2027 Best Colleges rankings , with Iowa universities appearing in categories like National Universities and National Liberal Arts Colleges.

U.S. News evaluated more than 1,700 U.S. colleges and universities based on 17 factors to measure academic quality and graduate success, according to the 2026 methodology. Criteria included graduation rate, first-year retention, and graduation performance rate, among other indicators, to determine the best school.

Here are the Iowa schools that made the rankings.

Which Iowa university ranked the best, according to U.S. News?

The University of Iowa was the state's only school to rank among the nation's top 100 National Universities, coming in a nine-way tie with schools such as the University of San Diego and Creighton University at No. 100.

Iowa improved in its standing after being ranked No. 102 in 2026 . Among public schools, Iowa was tied for No. 46 in the country.

Iowa State University was the second-best university in Iowa, rising to No. 116 in 2027 from No. 117 the previous year. ISU ranked No. 55 among public universities.

Here are the highest-ranking national universities in Iowa for 2026, according to U.S. News.

Other Iowa schools to receive recognition include the University of Northern Iowa , which was named the top public university in the Midwest; and Dordt University , which is the No. 6 private school in the Midwest.

Which Iowa liberal arts college ranked the best?

Grinnell College maintained its placement as the No. 1 liberal arts college in Iowa, according to U.S. News. Nationally, the college ranked No. 16. This is a drop from 2026 , when Grinnell ranked No. 13.

Here are the top-ranked Iowa liberal arts colleges in 2027, according to U.S. News.

Other Iowa colleges recognized in the rankings included Central College in Pella, Simpson College in Indianola and Wartburg College in Waverly, which were ranked 13th, eighth and seventh, respectively, among regional colleges in the Midwest.

articles.title: US treasury chief Scott Bessent could be Trump's new AI adviser amid US-China talks: Report
articles.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent could be President Donald Trump’s new artificial intelligence adviser, with his name emerging as a possible choice for
articles.body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent could be President Donald Trump’s new artificial intelligence adviser, with his name emerging as a possible choice for the administration’s proposed “AI czar” role as concerns grow in Washington over the risks posed by the rapidly developing technology.Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing a source familiar with the discussions, that Bessent could take up the role. The Treasury Department did not immediately comment on the possibility, while a second source told Reuters that no decision had been made. The development comes days after Trump said he would appoint an AI adviser and create an “AI force”.Why is Scott Bessent being considered?Bessent has recently played a key role in US-China discussions involving artificial intelligence. On Sunday, he led talks in New York with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of a planned meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.AI was among the major issues discussed during the talks. Bessent later said Washington had proposed creating a US-China AI dialogue, with a focus on national security concerns.The US also proposed an AI safety notification mechanism for incidents that could reach the level of a national security concern.Bessent’s involvement comes as Washington and Beijing increasingly link AI to economic and national security issues, including competition over advanced technology and computing capabilities.What is an ‘AI czar’?“AI czar” is an informal term generally used for a senior official tasked with coordinating a government’s artificial intelligence policy. It is not a formal Cabinet position established under US law.Trump announced on September 19 that he planned to appoint an AI adviser and create an “AI force”, but did not provide details about the structure, powers or responsibilities of the proposed body.It remains unclear whether the new role would primarily coordinate AI policy across federal agencies, focus on national security or have a wider mandate covering the technology sector.Trump’s stance on AI regulationTrump has repeatedly argued against additional regulations that he says could slow the growth of the US AI industry. His administration has emphasised developing AI while using existing criminal and civil laws to address harmful activity.The proposed AI force comes as lawmakers and policymakers in Washington debate how the US should address the risks associated with increasingly powerful AI systems without limiting technological development.What other roles does Bessent hold?Bessent, a former hedge fund manager, has already been given several high-profile responsibilities by Trump. He has played a leading role in the administration’s trade policy overhaul and has been involved in negotiations with Ukraine over critical minerals.He also temporarily headed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and is serving as acting commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service. The Treasury Department is also leading US efforts to economically isolate Iran through sanctions and other measures.Who held the AI czar role before?Bessent would not be the first Trump administration official associated with the AI czar title. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar before stepping down from the formal role in March and moving to an external advisory position.The possible selection of Bessent would come as AI takes on a growing role in US economic, technological, and national security discussions, particularly in Washington’s relationship with Beijing.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1934, a New York collector bought a Fabergé figure tied to Russia’s imperial court; nearly 80 years later it resurfaced in a family attic and sold at auction for a record $5.2 million
articles.summary: US News: A tiny figurine connected to Russia’s last imperial family spent nearly eight decades hidden from public view before emerging from a New York attic an.
articles.body: A tiny figurine connected to Russia’s last imperial family spent nearly eight decades hidden from public view before emerging from a New York attic and selling for $5.2 million at auction. The hardstone figure, created by the Fabergé workshop in 1912, depicts Nikolai N. Pustynnikov, a personal Cossack bodyguard to Empress Alexandra Feodorovna, wife of Emperor Nicholas II. It was discovered in 2013 in an attic in Rhinebeck, New York, decades after it had been purchased by an American collector in 1934.When the seven-inch figure was finally offered at Stair Galleries in Hudson, New York, on October 26, 2013, it had an estimated value of between $500,000 and $800,000. After around 15 minutes of intense bidding, however, the hammer price reached $5.2 million, setting a record for a Fabergé hardstone figure at auction at the time. Including the buyer’s commission, the total was reported at about $5.98 million.From Russia’s imperial court to a New York atticThe figure dates to the final years of the Russian Empire, when Fabergé produced highly detailed hardstone portraits of people and character types associated with imperial Russia.Pustynnikov served as a Kamer-Kazak, or Chamber Cossack, for Empress Alexandra Feodorovna. The bodyguards were non-commissioned officers taken from the Cossack regiments. Pustynnikov was born in the Cossack city of Novocherkassk, northeast of the Black Sea. He began his military service in 1876 and faithfully served Empress Alexandra from the time of her marriage to Emperor Nicholas II in 1894 until the Russian Revolution. Being appointed to attend a member of the Imperial family was a great honour and brought tremendous privileges. He was a highly esteemed servant who was closely identified with the Empress.In 1912, Emperor Nicholas II commissioned the figure of Pustynnikov for his wife, together with one of his brother's Cossacks, Andrei Kudinov, Kamer Kazak, as a gift to his mother, the Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna. Henry Bainbridge, Fabergé’s agent in London and biographer, wrote: "The Tsar Nicholas II commissioned Fabergé to make stone models of these guards. They were to be portraits from life, the two Cossacks attending at the Fabergé studios where they were modelled in wax."Fabergé says the figure was one of an exceptionally rare group of lifelike hardstone figures that attracted the attention of Emperor Nicholas II. The company says estimates have placed the number of such figurines produced at between 60 and 80, although Tatiana Fabergé, in 'Fabergé: A Comprehensive Reference Book', considered the actual number to be considerably lower.Portrait figures showing identifiable historical people are rarer still. Fabergé notes that these works are considered comparable in rarity to the famous Imperial Easter Eggs.The Pustynnikov figure itself is particularly distinctive. The design for the figure of Pustynnikov dated 31st January 1912 is contained in the design album of Fabergé’s Chief Workmaster Henrik Wigström. Although the production of the figure was supervised by Wigström, it was probably carved by either, Derbyshev or Kremlev, the master lapidaries. Theyworked from a wax model produced by the sculptor Boris Frödman-Cluzel. According to an art-market report, the seven-inch statuette features a coat made from nephrite and jasper, with gold and enamelled orders and medals. The boots bear Cyrillic inscriptions identifying Fabergé, the year 1912 and Pustynnikov’s position as a Kamer-Kazak dating back to 1894.Nearly 80 years out of sightThe figurine had already travelled a remarkable distance before reaching the attic. After the 1917 Revolution, the Imperial family's possessions were confiscated and the two Chamber Cossack figures ended up at Pavlovsk Palace. By 1925, the Pustynnikov figure had been sold to American industrialist and art dealer Armand Hammer, who later brought it to the United States. Hammer later sold it to George H. Davis, a Fabergé collector, in New York in 1934. After that transaction, the object eventually disappeared from public view.For decades, its whereabouts remained unknown. The trail was finally picked up when the piece was found in the attic of a deceased descendant of the collector in Rhinebeck. Importantly, the discovery was accompanied by documentation, including receipts that helped establish its history and connection to the 1934 purchase. That provenance helped transform what could have appeared to be an old decorative object into an important piece of Russian imperial art.A record-breaking auctionThe discovery came at a time when Fabergé’s rare hardstone figures were already attracting major interest from collectors. The previous auction record for a hardstone figure was $1.8 million, achieved at Sotheby’s in New York in 2005 for a figure depicting a boyar.The Pustynnikov figure more than doubled that price. The $5.2 million hammer price also demonstrated the premium attached to works that combine rarity, craftsmanship and a documented connection to the Romanov court. The figure was eventually purchased by London jeweller and Russian art dealer Wartski, which has a long history of dealing in Imperial Russian works of art.What began as a forgotten object in an Upstate New York attic therefore turned out to be a surviving fragment of the final years of Imperial Russia, carrying with it a trail that stretched from Fabergé’s workshop and the imperial court to a 1934 New York sale and, nearly 80 years later, one of the most remarkable antique discoveries to reach auction.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mystery surrounds German soldiers found near mud-covered WWII motorcycle in Danube
articles.summary: A Wehrmacht motorcycle and the remains of two German soldiers have emerged from the Danube River in Budapest more than 80 years after World War II ended.
articles.body: A relic of World War II has emerged from the Danube more than 80 years after the war ended — along with the remains of two German soldiers whose identities still remain a mystery. The Wehrmacht motorcycle — which officials identified as a DKW NZ 350-1 — was found in the Danube River in central Budapest this summer. The discovery was announced by the German War Graves Commission, an organization that works to locate, recover and identify German war dead, in August. WRECK OF DEADLIEST US NAVAL LOSS OF WORLD WAR I FOUND AFTER MORE THAN A CENTURY: 'LOST WITH ALL HANDS' Pictures show the heavily corroded motorcycle caked in mud and rust — with its frame, wheels, fuel tank and storage boxes still largely intact. "Because the harbor mud is mixed with gas oil, the motorcycle and identification tags are well preserved," the German War Graves Commission said in a statement, adding that the motorcycle model "was considered particularly robust and reliable at the time." Officials also found the remains of two German soldiers while recovering the motorcycle, along with two well-preserved identification tags. Both tags were still intact. Typically, one half of a fallen soldier's tag was left with the body, while the other was sent to the Wehrmacht Information Office so that the soldier's family could be notified, according to the commission. EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH The identification tags found with the remains are still being deciphered, Diane Tempel-Bornett, a spokesperson for the German War Graves Commission, told Fox News Digital in a translated email. Tempel-Bornett said that despite the discovery of the tags, the identities of the two soldiers remain unknown. "The fact that the identification tags were found with the dead does not necessarily mean that they belonged to them — although that is quite possible," she said. REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY The fact that the tags were still intact could indicate the soldiers were never recovered or officially accounted for after their deaths, Tempel-Bornett said. Tempel-Bornett said identifying the soldiers can be a "long, painstaking process," with even small details offering potential clues. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Investigators can glean clues from the remains, including height, age and possible origin, while personal belongings such as wedding rings, glasses, jewelry and papers can also help establish an identity. Researchers then compare those findings with military records and other historical evidence. "We can only speculate [on the cause of death]." "Here, we work closely with the German Federal Archives in Berlin," she added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Only when everything fits together is the person's fate considered to have been clarified." The final stage, Tempel-Bornett said, is to reach out to any relatives of the deceased. "If we have inquiries from relatives searching for them, that makes it easier," she said. "Otherwise, our colleagues try to do so through an inquiry with the residents' registration authorities." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For now, the identities of the two soldiers — and how they and the motorcycle came to rest in the Danube — are an ongoing mystery. "We can only speculate [on the cause of death]," added Tempel-Bornett.
