articles.title: Putin's party wins again as expected. So why does Russia still hold elections?
articles.summary: Europe News: Russians went to the polls. The votes were counted. Russian President Putin's party United Russia won again, and comfortably.The result itself was har.
articles.body: Russians went to the polls. The votes were counted. Russian President Putin's party United Russia won again, and comfortably.The result itself was hardly the mystery. The more interesting question is why Russia still goes through the elaborate business of elections when the system makes a genuine change of power extremely unlikely.Because in Russia, an election may not simply be about choosing who governs. It can also tell the Kremlin who is turning up, where support is weakening, which regional leaders can deliver and how well the machinery is working. But first, a simpler question: does a Russian vote actually matter?Putin's ruling United Russia party won 57.83% of the vote, according to Russia's Central Election Commission, with more than 95% of ballots counted. The result gives United Russia 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, preserving its constitutional majority. In the previous parliamentary election in 2021, the party officially received 49.8% of the vote.The election was also the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Putin had presented it as a test of support for his policies and the war. The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.That raises an obvious question: If Russia is widely described as an authoritarian or 'managed' political system, and the Kremlin is not seriously threatened by an opposition party taking power, why bother holding elections at all?Does a Russian vote actually matter?It would be too simplistic to say that an individual vote is completely meaningless simply because the ruling party is expected to win. Formally, an individual Russian vote can affect the composition of the Duma in two ways.Half of the 450 seats are distributed through nationwide party-list proportional representation, with a 5% threshold, while the other 225 are elected from single-member constituencies.The weight of an individual vote differs between the two.“In the party-list contest, one vote is a very small part of the national total, although collectively these votes determine 225 seats and can be particularly important when a party is near the 5% threshold,” explained foreign affairs expert Robinder Sachdev. “In a close constituency race, however, a relatively small number of votes can directly determine who wins that seat,” explained foreign expert he added.The 2026 result illustrates how strongly the constituency component can amplify a party's parliamentary strength.United Russia won 355 of the 450 seats, up from 343 in the previous Duma and the party's highest total so far.That gives the party well over the two-thirds threshold in the Duma. It can pass ordinary federal legislation without needing support from other parties and has enough votes for federal constitutional laws and the Duma stage of constitutional amendments.“So an individual vote has limited weight by itself, but aggregated votes — particularly in single-member constituencies — can have a major effect on the parliamentary balance of power,” Sachdev said.Does the vote count actually matter?In the narrowest sense, yes.Russians cast ballots, those ballots are counted and the resulting numbers determine how parliamentary seats are allocated. United Russia's 57.83% vote share is therefore not simply a number that has no connection whatsoever to voting.But whether voters have a meaningful opportunity to change who exercises power is a different question.Russia's political system has placed significant restrictions on genuine electoral competition. Reuters described the 2026 parliamentary election as taking place in a “tightly controlled political system” in which candidates opposed to Moscow's war in Ukraine have largely been excluded.Several parties besides United Russia are represented in the Duma, but Russia's parliamentary opposition operates within tightly drawn limits, with the major parties generally supporting Putin on key issues, including the war in Ukraine.According to the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Yabloko, a liberal party that opposed the Ukraine war and called for a ceasefire, was excluded from the federal parliamentary contest. CEPA said Yabloko's support among decided voters had risen to about 6% in the weeks before the election, compared with 1.2% in the 2021 election. Meanwhile, Putin critic Nikolai Bondarenko had already been barred from standing.So should this be called a gimmick?Not quite.Even when the broad political outcome is predictable, elections can serve several purposes for an authoritarian political system.Sachdev said elections provide formal electoral legitimacy while allowing the leadership to demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support.“Elections also help manage the political system itself,” Sachdev said, adding that they provide opportunities to renew parliament, accommodate different groups within the governing establishment and assess the performance of regional political organisations and officials.They also provide information.“The Kremlin may already have extensive polling and administrative data, but an actual election reveals the geography, intensity and organisational strength of support across the country,” he said.In other words, the Kremlin does not necessarily need an election to discover who rules Russia. It can use an election to find out how well the political machine is functioning.1. An election creates a claim of public supportThe first and most obvious purpose is legitimacy.The Kremlin can point to an electoral result and say that millions of Russians participated and that the governing party received a majority of votes.That does not settle the question of whether the election was free and fair. But politically, the existence of an official vote gives the government a concrete result with which to demonstrate public backing.This election is particularly significant because it took place during the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin has an interest in demonstrating that the war has not produced a political revolt at home.Sachdev said the election allows the Russian leadership to “demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support”, even if the broader political outcome is predictable.That distinction is important. An election can provide a government with an official measure of participation without necessarily providing an unrestricted contest for political power.2. It gives the Kremlin a measure of support — even if an imperfect oneThis is where the question of whether votes “count” becomes more complicated.Even in a tightly controlled election, authorities can learn something from participation. How many people turn out? Where is turnout unusually low? Which regions deliver particularly strong support? Where does United Russia perform worse than expected? Are local officials able to mobilise their populations?These are valuable pieces of information for an authoritarian government.A 2021 Carnegie analysis described Russian parliamentary elections as functioning less as contests over who would govern and more as a mechanism for measuring and demonstrating support for Putin's system.Sachdev said an election provides a different kind of information from opinion polls, intelligence reports or administrative data because it “tests behaviour and administrative capacity under real conditions.”“Turnout, abstention, regional variations and the performance of individual candidates can reveal where support is strong, where enthusiasm is weaker, and how effectively governors and local political organisations are able to mobilise voters,” he said.Moreover, information moving upwards through a political hierarchy can be filtered, because officials may have incentives to report favourable results to their superiors.Sachdev said an election can therefore provide an additional dataset against which those reports can be assessed. “Political-science research describes this as a ‘fire alarm’ function of elections,” he said.So the election does not simply measure public opinion. It gives the Kremlin a regional picture of both political sentiment and the effectiveness of the state and party machinery in mobilising voters.3. Elections keep political elites in lineThere is another audience for Russian elections that is often overlooked: the people inside the system.An election allows governors, mayors, party officials and other local power brokers to demonstrate that they can deliver the results expected by Moscow.Carnegie has described regional elections in Russia as an “initiation ritual” for governors and local elites — an opportunity for them to demonstrate control over their territories.Sachdev said regional leaders are expected not only to administer their territories but also to maintain political stability and demonstrate an ability to mobilise electoral support.Research on Russian regional politics has found that United Russia has historically performed better where governors command effective political organisations and local networks, he said.This means an election can function almost like an internal performance review. If a governor produces the desired result, it demonstrates political control.If a region suddenly records unexpectedly weak support for the ruling party, that can raise questions in Moscow about the governor's popularity, the effectiveness of the regional administration, the strength of the local party organisation or underlying economic and social dissatisfaction.An unexpectedly poor result would not automatically lead to a governor's removal. But, Sachdev said, electoral underperformance “can weaken a regional leader's standing with the federal centre” and become one factor in subsequent decisions about appointments, tenure or political advancement.So even if the Kremlin already knows which party will dominate parliament, the election can tell it how effectively its political network is operating below the national level.4. It gives voters a controlled way to participateThere is also a social function.Russia's government does not necessarily want every citizen to become politically disengaged. Voting gives people a formal mechanism for expressing preferences, even if the range of choices is restricted.The question is not necessarily whether the Kremlin believes Russians are choosing between two equally viable governments.Rather, elections can allow the system to channel political participation without allowing that participation to threaten the basic distribution of power.Sachdev said elections also help “renew the composition of parliament” and accommodate different groups within the governing establishment.This means that even where the election does not pose a serious threat to the ruling political system, it can still play a role in determining which individuals and factions occupy positions within that system.5. Elections can reveal dissatisfaction — but not necessarily change the governmentThis is perhaps the most counterintuitive part.A controlled election can still contain information about dissatisfaction.People can abstain. They can spoil ballots. They can vote for smaller parties or candidates. They can use whatever limited electoral choices are available to signal disagreement.Russia's political opposition has previously tried to use elections tactically to weaken United Russia, even when it could not realistically replace the Kremlin.But the ability to express dissatisfaction and the ability to translate that dissatisfaction into a change of government are two different things which is why the Kremlin may tolerate a certain degree of electoral competition while drawing firm limits around the political system.So, is the result meaningless?Not necessarily.The official vote count is meaningful as a description of what Russia's electoral authorities say happened. But the number cannot be read in isolation as a straightforward measure of Russians' freely expressed political preferences.The composition of the ballot matters. So does who was permitted to campaign, what political views could be openly expressed, the degree of media access available to competing forces, turnout and the broader electoral environment.This creates the central paradox of Russia's elections - The votes can be real without the contest being genuinely competitive. A Russian voter can make a choice. But the political system determines, to a significant extent, which choices are available in the first place. That is why the 57.83% figure needs to be read carefully. It is an official electoral result, but it is not equivalent to saying that 57.83% of all Russians freely chose Putin's political system.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
articles.summary: The tenant of the flat in Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the firm which recently bought it.
articles.body:
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.

The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.

Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.

However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.

It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.

Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.

Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.

Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.

In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".

The hard men removing squatters in Spain

'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic

Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons.

A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother."

"There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate."

In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home.

The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company.

The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead.

"Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.

A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes.

In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.

The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".

However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

articles.title: Israeli soldier accused of Gaza war crimes leaves India after complaint by Palestinian group: Report

articles.body: An Israeli soldier accused of alleged war crimes in Gaza has left India weeks after the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), a Palestinian rights group, filed a criminal complaint against him, according to a report by Middle East Eye.The soldier, whose identity has not been made public, left India in mid-September, a lawyer familiar with the case told Middle East Eye. It remains unclear whether the complaint influenced his departure or whether he left after completing his holiday.The development comes amid renewed calls for countries to uphold international law. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, speaking on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Monday, said multilateralism works best when international law, rules and norms are "scrupulously observed".Second Israeli soldier to leave India after complaintThe latest case marks the second incident this year in which the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has identified an Israeli soldier travelling in India and filed a complaint against him.In June, the Brussels-based organisation approached Indian authorities seeking the arrest of Eitan Gilboa, an Israeli military reservist who was vacationing in Himachal Pradesh. HRF accused Gilboa, who was identified as a member of the Israeli military's 271st Combat Engineering Battalion, of involvement in the demolition of civilian buildings in Khan Younis and Rafah.According to reports, HRF submitted material, including geolocated videos, social media posts and chain-of-command documentation to Indian authorities. Gilboa was subsequently traced by pro-Palestinian activists to locations including Old Manali and Gondla in Himachal Pradesh before leaving India.The latest case has followed a similar sequence, with HRF identifying an Israeli soldier through publicly available information, filing a complaint with Indian authorities and the individual subsequently leaving the country.India has long been a popular destination for young Israelis after their mandatory military service. Many undertake an extended post-service trip, commonly known as "tiul gadol", which can last several months.The trend has also contributed to the informal "Hummus Trail" followed by Israeli travellers across several Indian destinations, including Kasol, Dharamkot, Goa, Hampi, Gokarna, Kodaikanal, Rishikesh, Varanasi and Pushkar.Tourism has also featured in India-Israel bilateral cooperation. In February 2026, Israel allocated 4 million shekels for initiatives aimed at strengthening tourism ties with India.The HRF has increasingly sought to pursue legal complaints against Israeli military personnel over alleged conduct during Israel's military campaign in Gaza. The organisation's complaints have also brought attention to the presence of former and serving Israeli military personnel travelling in countries including India.Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin Uber driver arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting teen passenger in California; activated child locks to prevent him from leaving
articles.summary: US News: A 32-year-old rideshare driver in California has been arrested after allegedly sexually assaulting a teenage passenger during a ride in San Jose, with.
articles.body: A 32-year-old rideshare driver in California has been arrested after allegedly sexually assaulting a teenage passenger during a ride in San Jose, with investigators now warning that there could be additional victims.Police said the incident took place on the evening of September 12 in downtown San Jose. Officers responded to the 100 block of Paseo de San Antonio shortly after 10:30pm following a report of a sexual assault involving a minor.The juvenile male had been traveling in an Uber vehicle when the driver allegedly sexually assaulted him, according to the San Jose Police Department.The suspect was identified as Anuj Kumar, a 32-year-old resident of Foster City. According to NBC Bay Area, court records alleged that Kumar inappropriately touched the 14-year-old passenger and activated the vehicle's child locks, preventing him from leaving. The alleged assault took place near the teenager's destination, the Hammer Theatre close to San Jose State University.Police said the teenager contacted authorities immediately after getting out of the vehicle, allowing investigators to begin their investigation."We're fortunate that the victim reported this to the San Jose Police Department immediately so that we could begin our investigation," police spokesperson Stacie Shih said.Investigators used automated license-plate reader cameras to identify the vehicle involved and subsequently linked it to Kumar, police said. With assistance from the Foster City Police Department, Kumar was arrested in Foster City on September 13, a day after the alleged assault.Kumar was booked into the Santa Clara County Main Jail on suspicion of sexual assault of a minor.Court records said Kumar had worked as an Uber driver for about two-and-a-half years and had a 4.95 rating. Uber has permanently banned him from its platform following the allegations, the company said."What's been reported is deeply disturbing and has no place on our platform," an Uber spokesperson said, adding that the company was supporting law enforcement with the investigation.San Jose police are now investigating whether there may be other victims. Authorities have asked anyone who has information about Kumar or who experienced a similar incident to contact Detective Hoang of the San Jose Police Department's Sexual Assaults Investigation Unit at 408-277-4102 or 4684@sanjoseca.gov.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Eliminated major political danger': PLA mouthpiece hails removal of two top generals from CCP and Chinese military
articles.summary: The Chinese military's mouthpiece on Wednesday hailed the recent expulsion of two top generals from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People's
articles.body: The Chinese military's mouthpiece on Wednesday hailed the recent expulsion of two top generals from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People's Liberation Army (PLA), saying their removal would promote the “purity and honour” of the military and enable it to accomplish its missions and tasks.The CCP expelled Generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli from the party and military on Monday for "serious violations of discipline and the law."“The serious investigation and punishment of the two eliminated a major hidden political danger for the party and the military and constitutes a major victory in the military’s tough, protracted and overall battle against corruption,” PLA Daily, the mouthpiece of the Chinese military, said in a front-page editorial, referring to Zhang and Liu.“The PLA has thoroughly uncovered the lingering poisonous influences and accumulated ills, undergone tempering and forging from the inside out, which has ‘continuously improved the morale and spirit of the troops’,” the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post quoted the editorial as saying.The editorial further stated that the “international situation, national conditions and party and military conditions are all undergoing complex and profound changes” and therefore “we must unify our thinking and actions with the decisions and arrangements of the party Central Committee and the CMC”.The Central Military Commission (CMC) is the overall high command of the PLA, headed by Chinese President Xi Jinping.Zhang, 75, served as a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the CMC, while 61-year-old Liu served as a CMC member and chief of staff of the CMC's joint staff department. Zhang was also a member of the 24-man Politburo, the top decision-making body of the CPC.They are decorated war heroes and the only CMC members with combat experience. Both took part in PLA campaigns against Vietnam in the late 1970s.The sacking of Zhang, the highest-ranking military official, in particular, has sent shockwaves through the Chinese military establishment.Xi, since taking charge in 2012, has been publicly asserting that the country's military should function under CPC leadership and strictly follow its policies.Dozens of senior PLA officers have been sacked or punished under an intensified anti-corruption campaign carried out by Xi, which critics say consolidated his hold on power. It included two former defence ministers and dozens of senior PLA officers.(with PTI inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
